slides.title: Three decisions inside "train the network"
slides.notes: Draw a valley on the board. Mark a start point, a path and a stopping point.

runs.text: The first weights. A bad start can leave the network unable to learn anything at all.
The algorithm that moves the weights downhill. The choice changes training from hours to seconds.
Too early and it has not learnt. Too late and it has memorised the training examples.
Training is a walk downhill on the error surface. Today is about the first step, the stride and the last step.

slides.title: Why not start every weight at zero?
slides.notes: Zero is a saddle point of the performance surface. Ask the class to compute the gradient of a 1-2-1 network with all weights zero.

runs.text: Why not start every weight at zero?
The hidden neurons can never differ
With zero weights every hidden output is tansig(0) = 0, so the output layer receives nothing.
The slope for each hidden weight is multiplied by an output weight of zero: no update.
With equal non-zero weights, every hidden neuron gets the same update and stays an identical copy. Eight neurons behave as one.
Draw each weight at random, for example between −0.5 and 0.5 when inputs are normalised to [−1, 1].
Different starts break the symmetry: each neuron receives a different slope and learns a different feature.
Small values keep the sigmoids in their steep region, where learning is fast.

slides.title: Starting well: three more points
slides.notes: Nguyen-Widrow is the default initialisation for multilayer networks in the MATLAB toolbox. Each neuron begins by covering its own slice of the input range.

runs.text: Large weights push every neuron into its flat region. The slope there is nearly zero, so training crawls across a plateau.
Choose the size of the weights and spread the biases so that the active regions of the hidden neurons are distributed evenly across the input range.
Different starts end in different valleys. Train 5 to 10 times from new random weights and keep the network with the lowest validation error.
Never judge a design from a single training run.

slides.title: Different starts end in different places
slides.notes: In the mission game the Train stage has a "starts" control. Three starts are noticeably safer than one.

runs.text: Different starts end in different places
Same data, same network, three random starts
Start 2 settles in a poor local minimum and never recovers.
Starts 1 and 3 reach nearly the same error at different speeds.
The error surface of a multilayer network has many valleys.
Restarting is cheap insurance: keep the best on validation data.

slides.title: The training algorithms, compared
slides.notes: Resilient backpropagation (Rprop) is another common choice for pattern recognition. All of these were derived in Unit 3; today is about choosing.

rows.text: Straight down the slope, fixed learning rate α
Slow; α is hard to choose
Smooths the path; adapts the rate
Combines past directions; no line search
Slower than LM on small fits

runs.text: Rule of thumb: Levenberg-Marquardt for small fitting networks, scaled conjugate gradient for large or classification networks.

slides.title: The learning rate: slow, good or explosive
slides.notes: Recall from Unit 3: stable when alpha is less than 2 over the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian. This is why adaptive methods exist.

runs.text: The learning rate: slow, good or explosive
Steepest descent on a simple bowl
Too small: every step is safe but tiny. Thousands of iterations.
Too large: each step overshoots the bottom by more than the last. The error grows without limit.
The stable limit depends on the steepest curvature, which you do not know in advance.

slides.title: Levenberg-Marquardt in one line
slides.notes: Often converges in tens of iterations where steepest descent needs thousands. That is why the app uses it for the small fitting stations.

runs.text: J: Jacobian of the errors with respect to the weights. v: vector of errors. μ: the adjustable damping.
One knob, μ, blends two methods
Large μ: a small steepest-descent step. Safe when far from the minimum.
Small μ: a Gauss-Newton step. Very fast near the minimum.
If a step lowers the error, μ is divided; if it raises it, μ is multiplied and the step retried.
It must store and invert an n × n matrix: fine for hundreds of weights, not for millions.
It assumes a sum-of-squares error, so it suits fitting.

slides.title: Which algorithm for which job
slides.notes: Count for 64-30-10: 30(65) + 10(31) = 2,260 weights. The LM matrix would be 2,260 by 2,260.

runs.text: Up to a few hundred weights.
Mean square error with a linear output.
Example: a 2-8-1 network estimating delivery time from 200 orders.
Fastest and most accurate in this range.
Thousands of weights or more: memory grows only in step with the weights.
Works with cross-entropy and softmax outputs.
Example: a 64-30-10 digit recogniser with about 2,300 weights.
No learning rate to tune and no line search.
Sigmoid outputs in classification spend much of their time saturated, where the Levenberg-Marquardt approximation is poor.

slides.title: Four ways training ends
slides.notes: For SOM training the usual criterion is simply a fixed number of iterations. With Bayesian regularisation, train until the effective number of parameters settles.

rows.text: The size of the gradient falls below a small threshold
A flat point was reached: a minimum, or a plateau
The error falls below a target you set
Good enough for the purpose; no need to continue
A fixed number of iterations is used up
A safety limit. Training may not have converged
Validation error has risen for several checks in a row
Further training would only memorise. Keep the best weights

runs.text: Always record which criterion ended the run. "Maximum iterations" means: look again.

slides.title: Early stopping: let the validation set decide
slides.notes: The validation set is used for this decision, which is exactly why it cannot also be the test set.

runs.text: Early stopping: let the validation set decide
Stop at the lowest point of the validation curve
Both errors fall together at first: the network is learning the pattern.
Then training error keeps falling while validation error turns upward: it is now learning the noise.
Keep the weights from the validation minimum, not the last ones.
Wait a few checks before stopping, because the curve is bumpy.

slides.title: Zero start, then three learning rates
slides.notes: The answer to the question: the loss curve is flat from the first iteration, and the hidden neurons are identical.

runs.text: Zero start, then three learning rates
In Colab, set every weight to zero and train. The loss does not move. Print the hidden weights: all still equal.
Change to small random weights. The same network now learns.
Run three learning rates side by side: one crawls, one converges, one diverges to NaN.
With zero weights the code ran without any error message. How would you have known something was wrong?
